blocks.body:
Euclid's geometry is built with two idealised tools: a straightedge, with no marks on it, for drawing the line through two points, and a compass for drawing a circle with a given centre passing through a given point. With them you can bisect any angle, draw perpendiculars and parallels, and build regular triangles, squares, pentagons and hexagons. Three problems resisted for over two thousand years: construct a cube with twice the volume of a given cube; divide any angle into three equal parts; construct a square with the same area as a given circle.

All three are impossible, and the reason is algebraic. This page first shows what the tools can do, with proofs by congruent triangles from [[euclid-basics]] and power of a point from [[circles]], and then turns constructions into algebra using [[fields-ext]].

blocks.title: The basic constructions
blocks.body:
Each construction comes with a reason it works.

1. Perpendicular bisector of $AB$. Draw the circle centred $A$ through $B$ and the circle centred $B$ through $A$; they meet at $X$ and $Y$. Then $XA = XB$ and $YA = YB$, and the points equidistant from $A$ and $B$ form the perpendicular bisector, so the line $XY$ is it. It also gives the midpoint of $AB$.
2. Bisecting angle $\angle AOB$. The circle centred $O$ through $A$ meets ray $OB$ at $B'$. Construct the perpendicular bisector of $AB'$; it passes through $O$ (since $OA = OB'$), and by symmetry it bisects the angle.
3. Perpendicular to a line $\ell$ through a point $P$. Draw a circle centred $P$ meeting $\ell$ at two points; their perpendicular bisector passes through $P$ and is perpendicular to $\ell$.
4. Parallel to $\ell$ through $P$. Draw the perpendicular $m$ to $\ell$ through $P$, then the perpendicular to $m$ through $P$.
5. Transferring a length. The compass as described collapses when lifted, but Euclid showed (his second proposition) that a length can still be copied to any point, so we may use the compass with a radius equal to any constructed distance.
6. Dividing $AB$ into $n$ equal parts. Mark $n$ equal steps along any ray from $A$, ending at $C_n$; join $C_n$ to $B$ and draw parallels through the other marks. By the intercept theorem they cut $AB$ into equal parts.

The equilateral triangle, the square and the regular hexagon follow directly (a hexagon is six radius-length chords around a circle).

blocks.title: From points to numbers
blocks.body:
Fix two points $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ to set the unit of length. Call a point constructible if it can be reached from these two by a finite sequence of lines and circles, each new point being an intersection of lines or circles already drawn. Call a real number $x$ constructible if the point $(x, 0)$ is.

Which numbers do we get? Lengths can be added and subtracted along a line by copying them. Products and quotients come from similar triangles: on one ray from $O$ mark $OU = 1$ and $OA = a$, on another ray mark $OB = b$; the parallel to $UB$ through $A$ meets the second ray at a point $C$ with $OC = ab$, because triangles $OUB$ and $OAC$ are similar. Swapping roles gives $b/a$.

Square roots come from a circle. Put $A$, $B$, $C$ on a line with $AB = a$ and $BC = 1$, draw the circle on diameter $AC$, and erect the perpendicular at $B$, meeting the circle at $D$. By power of a point (or similar triangles), $BD^2 = AB\cdot BC = a$, so $BD = \sqrt a$.

So starting from 1 we can reach every number built from integers by $+, -, \times, \div$ and $\sqrt{\ }$, such as $\sqrt{2 + \sqrt3} - \frac{1}{\sqrt5}$. The striking fact is that nothing else is reachable.

blocks.title: Characterisation of constructible numbers
blocks.body:
A real number $x$ is constructible if and only if there is a chain of fields
$$\mathbb{Q} = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_n \subset \mathbb{R}, \qquad K_i = K_{i-1}(\sqrt{d_i}) \text{ with } d_i \in K_{i-1},\ d_i > 0,$$
such that $x \in K_n$. Consequently, if $x$ is constructible then $[\mathbb{Q}(x):\mathbb{Q}]$ is a power of 2.

The previous section shows the constructible numbers contain $\mathbb{Q}$ and are closed under the field operations and under square roots of positive numbers, so every element of such a $K_n$ is constructible.

For the converse, suppose every point drawn so far has both coordinates in a subfield $F$ of $\mathbb{R}$. A line through two such points has an equation $\alpha x + \beta y = \gamma$ with $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in F$. A circle with centre $(p,q)$ through $(s,t)$ has equation $x^2 + y^2 - 2px - 2qy + c = 0$ with $c = 2ps + 2qt - s^2 - t^2 \in F$. Now look at the new intersection points.

- Two lines: solving two linear equations needs only $+, -, \times, \div$, so the intersection has coordinates in $F$.
- A line and a circle: solve the line's equation for one variable and substitute. This gives a quadratic equation with coefficients in $F$, whose roots lie in $F(\sqrt D)$, where $D \in F$ is its discriminant ($D \ge 0$ since the intersection is real). The other coordinate then also lies in $F(\sqrt D)$.
- Two circles: subtracting their equations removes $x^2 + y^2$ and leaves a linear equation, so the intersection points are those of a line and a circle.

So each new point has coordinates in $F$ or in $F(\sqrt D)$ for some positive $D \in F$. Starting with $F = \mathbb{Q}$ and following the construction step by step gives the required chain, and $x$, a coordinate of a constructed point, lies in its last field.

Finally each step has $[K_i : K_{i-1}] = 1$ or 2, so $[K_n : \mathbb{Q}] = 2^m$ by the tower law. Since $\mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{Q}(x) \subseteq K_n$, the degree $[\mathbb{Q}(x):\mathbb{Q}]$ divides $2^m$, so it is a power of 2.

blocks.title: The three classical problems
blocks.body:
Doubling the cube. A cube of side 1 has volume 1; doubling it needs side $\sqrt[3]2$. This number is a root of $x^3 - 2$, which has no rational roots (the only candidates are $\pm1$ and $\pm2$). A cubic with no rational root has no linear factor over $\mathbb{Q}$, so it is irreducible, and $[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]2):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$. This is not a power of 2, so $\sqrt[3]2$ is not constructible.

Trisecting the angle. Some angles can be trisected (a right angle, since $30^\circ$ is constructible), but not all. An angle $\theta$ can be drawn exactly when $\cos\theta$ is constructible (drop a perpendicular from a point of the unit circle). The $60^\circ$ angle is constructible, so it suffices to show $\cos 20^\circ$ is not. From $\cos3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta$ with $\theta = 20^\circ$ we get $4c^3 - 3c = \frac12$, so $y = 2c$ satisfies $y^3 - 3y - 1 = 0$. The candidates $y = \pm 1$ fail ($1 - 3 - 1 = -3$ and $-1 + 3 - 1 = 1$), so this cubic is irreducible, $2\cos 20^\circ$ has degree 3, and $\cos20^\circ$ is not constructible.

Squaring the circle. A square of area $\pi$ has side $\sqrt\pi$; if it were constructible, so would be $\pi$, which would then be algebraic (a root of a nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients). Lindemann proved in 1882 that $\pi$ is transcendental, so this is impossible too. His proof is much harder and is not given here.

blocks.title: Regular polygons and a glimpse further
blocks.body:
A regular $n$-gon can be constructed exactly when the angle $\frac{2\pi}{n}$ can, that is, when $\cos\frac{2\pi}{n}$ is constructible. Gauss found in 1796 that the 17-gon is constructible, and the full answer (Gauss, with the converse completed by Wantzel in 1837) is: the regular $n$-gon is constructible if and only if $n = 2^k p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r$ where the $p_i$ are distinct Fermat primes, primes of the form $2^{2^j} + 1$. Only five are known: 3, 5, 17, 257, 65537; Euler showed $2^{32} + 1 = 641 \cdot 6700417$. For $3 \le n \le 20$ the constructible ones are $n = 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 16, 17, 20$. The full proof uses [[galois]] theory and [[cyclotomic]] fields.

Other tools give other answers. The compass alone can construct every point that straightedge and compass can (Mohr–Mascheroni), and a straightedge with one given circle and its centre suffices too (Poncelet–Steiner). A marked ruler (a neusis construction, used by Archimedes) or paper folding can trisect angles and double the cube, because those tools can solve cubic equations.

blocks.title: The regular pentagon
blocks.body: Show that $\cos 72^\circ = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4}$, and deduce that the regular pentagon is constructible.
blocks.solution:
Let $\theta = 72^\circ$ and $c = \cos\theta$. Since $5\theta = 360^\circ$, we have $3\theta = 360^\circ - 2\theta$, so $\cos3\theta = \cos2\theta$. Using $\cos3\theta = 4c^3 - 3c$ and $\cos2\theta = 2c^2 - 1$:
$$4c^3 - 2c^2 - 3c + 1 = 0, \qquad (c - 1)(4c^2 + 2c - 1) = 0.$$
Since $c \ne 1$, $c$ is a root of $4c^2 + 2c - 1 = 0$, and as $c > 0$, $c = \frac{-2 + \sqrt{20}}{8} = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4}$.

This number is built from integers by a square root and field operations, so it is constructible: construct $\sqrt5$ as the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 1 and 2, subtract 1, and divide by 4. Then mark the point at that distance from the centre of a unit circle along a radius, erect the perpendicular there to cut the circle; the chord from it to the end of the radius is a side of the regular pentagon.

blocks.title: The regular heptagon is impossible
blocks.body: Show that $\alpha = 2\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}$ satisfies $\alpha^3 + \alpha^2 - 2\alpha - 1 = 0$, and deduce that the regular 7-gon cannot be constructed.
blocks.solution:
Let $\zeta = \cos\frac{2\pi}{7} + i\sin\frac{2\pi}{7}$ (see [[complex-numbers]]), so $\zeta^7 = 1$, $\zeta \ne 1$ and $\alpha = \zeta + \zeta^{-1}$. Since $\zeta^7 - 1 = (\zeta - 1)(\zeta^6 + \cdots + \zeta + 1)$, we get $1 + \zeta + \zeta^2 + \cdots + \zeta^6 = 0$. Dividing by $\zeta^3$:
$$(\zeta^3 + \zeta^{-3}) + (\zeta^2 + \zeta^{-2}) + (\zeta + \zeta^{-1}) + 1 = 0.$$
Now $\alpha^2 = \zeta^2 + \zeta^{-2} + 2$ and $\alpha^3 = \zeta^3 + \zeta^{-3} + 3\alpha$. Substituting, $(\alpha^3 - 3\alpha) + (\alpha^2 - 2) + \alpha + 1 = 0$, which is $\alpha^3 + \alpha^2 - 2\alpha - 1 = 0$.

The only possible rational roots are $\pm1$, giving $-1$ and $1$, not 0. So the cubic is irreducible, $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$, and $\alpha$ is not constructible. Hence neither is $\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}$, and the heptagon cannot be constructed. This agrees with Gauss–Wantzel, since 7 is not a Fermat prime.

blocks.title: A square in a triangle
blocks.body: Given a triangle $ABC$ whose angles at $B$ and $C$ are acute, construct a square with two vertices on $BC$, one on $AB$ and one on $AC$.
blocks.solution:
Idea: draw a square with three of the four conditions, then enlarge it from $B$.

Choose any point $P$ on $AB$ between $A$ and $B$, and drop the perpendicular $PQ$ to $BC$. On $BC$, on the side of $Q$ away from $B$, mark $R$ with $QR = QP$, and complete the square $PQRS$ (perpendicular to $BC$ at $R$, of length $QP$). This square has $P$ on $AB$ and $Q, R$ on $BC$, but $S$ is probably not on $AC$.

Draw the line $BS$ and let it meet $AC$ at $S'$. The enlargement (homothety) with centre $B$ that sends $S$ to $S'$ maps lines through $B$ to themselves, so it sends $Q$ and $R$ to points of line $BC$ and $P$ to a point of line $AB$. It sends the square $PQRS$ to a square $P'Q'R'S'$, since enlargements preserve angles and multiply all lengths by the same factor. So $P'Q'R'S'$ has two vertices on $BC$, one on $AB$ and its fourth vertex $S'$ on $AC$, as required. (The acute angles ensure the square sits inside the triangle with $Q'$, $R'$ on the segment $BC$.)

Every step uses only perpendiculars, copied lengths and intersections, so it is a valid construction.

blocks.body:
- An impossibility proof is about exact constructions with finitely many steps. Approximate constructions, as accurate as you like, exist for everything.
- The marks matter: a straightedge with two marks on it is a different tool, and with it trisection is possible.
- The degree condition is necessary, not sufficient. Some numbers of degree 4 over $\mathbb{Q}$ are not constructible; the precise test is that the Galois group of the minimal polynomial has order a power of 2.
- Impossibility of trisection means no single method trisects every angle. Particular angles such as $90^\circ$ or $180^\circ$ can be trisected.
- A cubic with rational coefficients is irreducible exactly when it has no rational root, but for quartics and higher, having no rational root does not imply irreducibility: $(x^2 + 1)^2$ has no rational root.

The algebra behind this page is [[fields-ext]] and the tower law; the complete theory of which numbers and polygons are constructible is a chapter of [[galois]] theory, with the polygon question living in [[cyclotomic]] fields. The rational root test used here, and other irreducibility tests such as Eisenstein's criterion, are in [[integer-polynomials]] and [[polynomials-roots]]. The enlargement trick of the last example is a transformation in the sense of [[geo-transformations]].

1. Construct a segment of length $\sqrt3$ starting from a unit segment, and explain why your construction works.
2. Show that $\cos 15^\circ$ is constructible by writing it with square roots.
3. Prove that the regular 9-gon is not constructible.
4. Given two segments of lengths $a$ and $b$, construct a segment of length $\sqrt{ab}$, the geometric mean.
